AT-WILL EMPLOYMENT PRESUMPTION AND IMPLIED-IN-FACT CONTRACT LIMITS ON TERMINATION (LABOR CODE § 2922; GUZ V. BECHTEL) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

AT-WILL PRESUMPTION AND IMPLIED-IN-FACT CONTRACT LIMITS — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., recorded here as beginning on March 3, 2014 and ending on August 28, 2026. It describes what California's Labor Code and the California Supreme Court have said about the default rule that employment with no specified term may be ended at the will of either party (Labor Code section 2922), about how the parties to an employment relationship can depart from that default by an express or implied-in-fact agreement limiting the employer's right to terminate, about the kinds of evidence courts consider when deciding whether such an implied agreement exists, and about the limits of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing as a separate source of protection. Whether Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. actually reached any understanding that departed from at-will employment, what Acme, Inc.'s personnel documents said, and why the employment ended on August 28, 2026 are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and dates here does not itself establish that any of the rules described below applies to their relationship, and this sheet states what the statute and the courts have said rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular separation.

THE STATUTORY DEFAULT: EMPLOYMENT WITH NO SPECIFIED TERM IS TERMINABLE AT THE WILL OF EITHER PARTY
Labor Code section 2922 states the default rule for California employment relationships: an employment that has no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other, and "employment for a specified term" means employment for a period greater than one month. In Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000), the California Supreme Court described what that default means in practice — an at-will employment may be ended by either party "at any time without cause," for any or no reason, subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice — and, in the part of the opinion addressing the implied covenant of good faith, stated the consequence bluntly: where the presumption applies, the employer may act peremptorily, arbitrarily, or inconsistently, without providing protections such as prior warning, fair procedures, objective evaluation, or preferential reassignment. The court characterized this statutory presumption as "strong." As applied to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., this clause states the default from which the analysis in the following clauses begins; whether that default was displaced by an express or implied agreement is a separate question those clauses address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2922 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 2922 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2922.)
  "An at-will employment may be ended by either party “at any time without cause,” for any or no reason, and subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 335 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Labor Code section 2922 establishes the presumption that an employer may terminate its employees at will, for any or no reason. A fortiori, the employer may act peremptorily, arbitrarily, or inconsistently, without providing specific protections such as prior warning, fair procedures, objective evaluation, or preferential reassignment."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 350 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "While the statutory presumption of at-will employment is strong, it is subject to several limitations."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 335 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  Known gap: This clause combines the statutory text of Labor Code section 2922 with the California Supreme Court's description of the at-will default in Guz. It is real evidence of what the default rule is, not a claim that any particular employee is or was at-will, and not a claim that the default is unlimited: Guz itself immediately notes that the presumption "is subject to several limitations," and California has separate statutory and common-law rules (for example, anti-discrimination and anti-retaliation statutes, and the tort of wrongful termination in violation of public policy) that restrict the reasons for which even an at-will employee may be discharged; those are addressed in other documents in this corpus, not here. The Guz quotations come from the opinion's discussion of Labor Code section 2922 in Part III.A and from its discussion of the implied covenant in Part III.C; the second quotation describes the employer's latitude under the presumption "a fortiori" as a step in the court's reasoning about the covenant, and is reproduced here for what it says about the presumption. Quote-verification note: the Guz text was retrieved from CourtListener's html_with_citations field, whose typographic quotation marks and apostrophes are reproduced in the quotes below.

THE PRESUMPTION YIELDS TO THE PARTIES’ ACTUAL AGREEMENT: ANY OTHERWISE-LAWFUL LIMIT ON TERMINATION RIGHTS MAY BE AGREED TO
Guz explains that the section 2922 presumption governs only where the employer and employee "have reached no other understanding." Because the employment relationship is fundamentally contractual, the statute does not overcome the parties' freedom of contract to depart from at-will employment, and it does not prevent them from agreeing to any limitation, otherwise lawful, on the employer's termination rights. The court described the range of what can be agreed: the parties may define for themselves what cause or causes will permit termination, may specify the procedures under which termination shall occur, and may restrict the employer's termination rights more in some situations while leaving the employer freer in others. One familiar example is an agreement that the employee will be discharged only for "good cause," which the court, quoting its earlier decision in Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co., described as "a fair and honest cause or reason, regulated by good faith," as opposed to one that is "trivial, capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual." Whether Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee reached any such understanding — express or implied — is a question of fact this clause does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Thus, though Labor Code section 2922 prevails where the employer and employee have reached no other understanding, it does not overcome their “fundamental . . . freedom of contract” to depart from at-will employment."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "The statute does not prevent the parties from agreeing to any limitation, otherwise lawful, on the employer’s termination rights."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "The parties may define for themselves what cause or causes will permit an employee’s termination and may specify the procedures under which termination shall occur. The agreement may restrict the employer’s termination rights to a greater degree in some situations, while leaving the employer freer to act as it sees fit in others."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "a fair and honest cause or reason, regulated by good faith"
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317 (quoting Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 454, 467), 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "trivial, capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual"
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317 (quoting Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 454, 467), 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  Known gap: This is the California Supreme Court's own statement of the contractual character of the at-will presumption and of the parties' freedom to modify it, used as real evidence of that principle — not a claim that any particular employer and employee did agree to a limit on termination rights. The court's phrasing ("otherwise lawful") signals that some agreed limits could themselves be unlawful; this clause does not catalogue which. The "good cause" definition is quoted as Guz itself quoted it from Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 454; the Scott opinion was not independently fetched for this document, and the two short quotations below are taken from within a nested quotation in Guz (the opinion uses layered quotation marks and ellipses around them, which have been omitted by quoting only the inner words). The clause also does not address the separate question — decided in Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93 — of what a factfinder decides when an employer with a good-cause obligation discharges an employee for misconduct the employee denies; the Cotran opinion was not retrieved for this document and its holding is not described here.

AN AGREEMENT LIMITING TERMINATION NEED NOT BE EXPRESS: THE IMPLIED-IN-FACT CONTRACT AND THE FOLEY FACTORS
The agreement that displaces at-will status does not have to be written or even spoken. Guz confirms that the contractual understanding "may be implied in fact, arising from the parties' conduct evidencing their actual mutual intent to create such enforceable limitations." The kinds of evidence that bear on whether such an implied agreement exists, and what its content is, were identified by the California Supreme Court in Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988), which drew them from the Court of Appeal's earlier decision in Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc. (1981): the personnel policies or practices of the employer, the employee's longevity of service, actions or communications by the employer reflecting assurances of continued employment, and the practices of the industry in which the employee is engaged. Foley added that, under Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary the relationship is terminable at any time without cause — but that when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, section 2922 does not diminish the force of those obligations. As applied here, these are the categories of evidence a court would look to in deciding whether Acme, Inc.'s conduct toward Jordan Lee between March 3, 2014 and August 28, 2026 evidenced an actual mutual understanding limiting termination; the clauses that follow describe how Guz said that evidence is weighed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The contractual understanding need not be express, but may be implied in fact, arising from the parties’ conduct evidencing their actual mutual intent to create such enforceable limitations."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 336 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "In the employment context, factors apart from consideration and express terms may be used to ascertain the existence and content of an employment agreement, including "the personnel policies or practices of the employer, the employee's longevity of service, actions or communications by the employer reflecting assurances of continued employment, and the practices of the industry in which the employee is engaged.""
  — Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654 (quoting Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc. (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 311, 327), 47 Cal.3d 654, 680 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1170824/foley-v-interactive-data-corp/)
  "Pursuant to Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary, the relationship is terminable at any time without cause. But when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, Labor Code section 2922 does not diminish the force of such contractual or legal obligations."
  — Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654, 47 Cal.3d 654, 680 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1170824/foley-v-interactive-data-corp/)
  Known gap: This clause pairs Guz's statement that the limiting agreement may be implied in fact with Foley's list of the factors relevant to finding one. Both are real evidence of the governing doctrine; neither is a claim that any given combination of facts establishes an implied contract — Guz specifically cautions against treating the factors mechanically, as a later clause explains. The Foley factor list is itself a quotation from Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc. (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 311, 327; the Pugh opinion was not independently fetched for this document, and the factors are quoted as they appear in Foley's own text (which uses straight apostrophes, e.g., "employee's"). The Foley passage on section 2922 carries a footnote marker (23) after "obligations" in the source; the footnote was not retrieved and is not described here.

THE FACTORS ARE WEIGHED FOR WHAT THEY SHOW ABOUT THE PARTIES’ ACTUAL UNDERSTANDING — NOT “SHAKEN TOGETHER IN A BAG”
Guz clarified how the Foley factors operate. Foley had said the "totality of the circumstances" must be examined; Guz explained that this does not mean that any vague combination of factors, "shaken together in a bag," necessarily allows a finding that the employee could be discharged only for good cause. Instead, courts "seek to enforce the actual understanding" of the parties, and the exact terms to which they assented — whether by express words or by conduct evidencing a similar meeting of minds — receive equally precise scrutiny. The court then stated the operative test for cases with no express agreement: every case turns on its own facts; the issue is whether the other evidence of the parties' conduct has a "tendency in reason" to demonstrate the existence of an actual mutual understanding on particular terms and conditions of employment; if that evidence logically permits conflicting inferences, a question of fact is presented; but where the undisputed facts negate the existence or breach of the claimed contract, summary judgment is proper. Whether the evidence concerning Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. would permit conflicting inferences is a question this clause describes but does not answer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "We did not suggest, however, that every vague combination of Foley factors, shaken together in a bag, necessarily allows a finding that the employee had a right to be discharged only for good cause, as determined in court."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 337 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Whether that understanding arises from express mutual words of agreement, or from the parties’ conduct evidencing a similar meeting of minds, the exact terms to which the parties have assented deserve equally precise scrutiny."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 337 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Every case thus turns on its own facts. Where there is no express agreement, the issue is whether other evidence of the parties’ conduct has a “tendency in reason” (Evid. Code, § 210) to demonstrate the existence of an actual mutual understanding on particular terms and conditions of employment. If such evidence logically permits conflicting inferences, a question of fact is presented."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 337 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "But where the undisputed facts negate the existence or the breach of the contract claimed, summary judgment is proper."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 337 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  Known gap: This is the California Supreme Court's own explanation of how the implied-contract inquiry is conducted, used as real evidence of the standard — not a prediction of how any particular set of facts would come out. The court's reference to Evidence Code section 210 (which defines relevant evidence in terms of a "tendency in reason") is reproduced from the opinion; section 210 was not independently fetched for this document. The summary-judgment sentence reflects the procedural posture of Guz (review of a summary judgment) and states when that procedure is proper, not what a jury would find at trial.

LONG SERVICE, RAISES, PROMOTIONS, AND GOOD REVIEWS DO NOT, BY THEMSELVES, CREATE AN IMPLIED CONTRACT NOT TO TERMINATE AT WILL
One of Guz's most-cited holdings concerns the "longevity of service" factor. John Guz had worked for Bechtel for over twenty years with steady raises, promotions, commendations, and good performance reviews, and argued that this record was strong evidence of an implied contract for permanent employment except upon good cause. The California Supreme Court agreed with a line of post-Foley Court of Appeal decisions that such events are "but natural consequences of a well-functioning employment relationship" and held that an employee's mere passage of time in the employer's service — even where marked with tangible indicia that the employer approves the employee's work — cannot alone form an implied-in-fact contract that the employee is no longer at will. Absent other evidence of the employer's intent, the court said, longevity, raises and promotions "are their own rewards" and do not, in and of themselves, constitute a contractual guarantee of future employment security; a contrary rule "would discourage the retention and promotion of employees." The court was equally clear that long service is not irrelevant: over an employee's tenure the employer can communicate, by its written and unwritten policies and practices or by informal assurances, that seniority and longevity do create rights against termination at will, and the issue is whether the employer's words or conduct, on which the employee reasonably relied, gave rise to that specific understanding. The length of Jordan Lee's service with Acme, Inc. from March 3, 2014 to August 28, 2026 is therefore a fact this doctrine treats as relevant only in combination with such words or conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "We agree that an employee’s mere passage of time in the employer’s service, even where marked with tangible indicia that the employer approves the employee’s work, cannot alone form an implied-in-fact contract that the employee is no longer at will. Absent other evidence of the employer’s intent, longevity, raises and promotions are their own rewards for the employee’s continuing valued service; they do not, in and of themselves, additionally constitute a contractual guarantee of future employment security. A rule granting such contract rights on the basis of successful longevity alone would discourage the retention and promotion of employees."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 341-342 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "These decisions reason that such events are but natural consequences of a well-functioning employment relationship, and thus have no special tendency to prove that the employer’s at-will implied agreement, reasonably understood as such by the employee, has become one that limits the employer’s future termination rights."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 341 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Length of employment is a relevant consideration but six years and nine months is sufficient time for conduct to occur on which a trier of fact could find the existence of an implied contract."
  — Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654, 47 Cal.3d 654, 681 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1170824/foley-v-interactive-data-corp/)
  "On the other hand, long and successful service is not necessarily irrelevant to the existence of such a contract. Over the period of an employee’s tenure, the employer can certainly communicate, by its written and unwritten policies and practices, or by informal assurances, that seniority and longevity do create rights against termination at will. The issue is whether the employer’s words or conduct, on which an employee reasonably relied, gave rise to that specific understanding."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 342 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  Known gap: This is the California Supreme Court's holding on the weight of longevity, raises, promotions, and favorable reviews, used as real evidence of that rule — not a determination that any particular employee's service record does or does not support an implied contract. The court's characterization of the post-Foley Court of Appeal decisions (Horn, Kovatch, Davis, Tollefson, Miller) is reproduced as Guz summarized them; those decisions were not independently fetched. Guz also expressly declined to read Foley as holding that long service alone suffices, explaining that Foley's own plaintiff had alleged "repeated oral assurances of job security" in addition to six years and nine months of service; Foley's own sentence on length of service is quoted below from the Foley text, and Guz's discussion of it is summarized in the body. Quote-verification note: the retrieved text places a page-break marker ("*342") inside the first quoted sentence between "approves" and "the employee's"; the quote below omits that marker, and the comparison was made after removing page-number markup.

HANDBOOK AT-WILL DISCLAIMERS AND WRITTEN PERSONNEL POLICIES: BOTH ARE EVIDENCE, NEITHER IS AUTOMATICALLY CONTROLLING
Guz addressed two kinds of employer documents that often point in opposite directions. Bechtel's written policy stated that its employees had no agreements guaranteeing continuous service and could be terminated at the company's option, and Bechtel argued this disclaimer conclusively reinforced the statutory presumption. The court held that an express disclaimer, reinforced by the presumption, satisfied the employer's initial burden on summary judgment, but did not necessarily foreclose the employee from proving an implied agreement: disclaimer language in a handbook or policy manual "does not necessarily mean an employee is employed at will." At the same time, such a disclaimer cannot be ignored — like any direct expression of employer intent communicated to employees and intended to apply to them, it must be taken into account along with all other pertinent evidence in ascertaining the terms of employment. Conversely, the court recognized that an employer's written personnel policies "may be an important source of implied-contract evidence," adding that when an employer promulgates formal personnel policies in handbooks, manuals, and memoranda disseminated to employees, "a strong inference may arise" that the employer intended workers to rely on them as terms and conditions of employment and that employees reasonably did so, and reiterating Foley's statement that a trier of fact can infer an agreement to limit the grounds for termination based on the employee's reasonable reliance on the company's personnel manual or policies. On the facts before it, the court found triable evidence that Bechtel's written personnel documents set forth implied contractual limits on the circumstances of termination, while also holding that those documents did not restrict Bechtel's freedom to reorganize and reduce its work force: Bechtel had "the absolute right" to eliminate Guz's work unit even if the decision was influenced by dissatisfaction with the unit's performance and even if the documents entitled an individual employee to progressive discipline before being fired for poor performance. What Acme, Inc.'s handbook, policies, and disclaimers (if any) said, and whether Jordan Lee reasonably relied on them, are facts this clause does not establish.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "This express disclaimer, reinforced by the statutory presumption of at-will employment, satisfied Bechtel’s initial burden, if any, to show that Guz’s claim of a contract limiting Bechtel’s termination rights had no merit. But neither the disclaimer nor the statutory presumption necessarily foreclosed Guz from proving the existence and breach of such an agreement."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 339 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "We agree that disclaimer language in an employee handbook or policy manual does not necessarily mean an employee is employed at will."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 340 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Like any direct expression of employer intent, communicated to employees and intended to apply to them, such language must be taken into account, along with all other pertinent evidence, in ascertaining the terms on which a worker was employed."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 340 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "As Guz suggests, an employer’s written personnel policies may be an important source of implied-contract evidence."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 344 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "When an employer promulgates formal personnel policies and procedures in handbooks, manuals, and memoranda disseminated to employees, a strong inference may arise that the employer intended workers to rely on these policies as terms and conditions of their employment, and that employees did reasonably so rely."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 344 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "the trier of fact can infer an agreement to limit the grounds for termination based on the employee’s reasonable reliance on the company’s personnel manual or policies."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317 (quoting Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654, 681-682), 24 Cal.4th 317, 344 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Bechtel had the absolute right to eliminate Guz’s work unit and to transfer the unit’s responsibilities to another company entity, even if the decision was influenced by dissatisfaction with the eliminated unit’s performance, and even if the personnel documents entitled an individual employee to progressive discipline procedures before being fired for poor performance."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 338 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  Known gap: This clause reports the California Supreme Court's treatment of handbook disclaimers and written personnel policies as real evidence of how such documents are weighed — not a claim about what any particular employer's documents provide or whether an employee relied on them. The court's discussion of out-of-state and lower-court authority on handbook disclaimers (Thomka, Walker, Wilkerson, Wood, and others) is reflected only through the court's own summary and was not independently fetched. The sentence about reasonable reliance on a personnel manual is Guz quoting Foley (47 Cal.3d at pp. 681-682); it is quoted here as it appears in the Guz text. The quoted "absolute right" sentence reflects the court's reading of Bechtel's specific personnel documents, which did not address reorganizations; it is not a general rule that written policies can never limit an employer's reorganization decisions. Guz left for the Court of Appeal on remand whether Bechtel breached the fair-layoff provisions (objective ranking, placement assistance) in its written policies; that question was not decided in the opinion quoted here.

THE IMPLIED COVENANT OF GOOD FAITH ADDS NO TERMINATION LIMITS BEYOND THE CONTRACT ITSELF, AND ITS BREACH YIELDS ONLY CONTRACT REMEDIES
Every California contract, including an employment contract, carries an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Guz explained why that covenant cannot itself supply the job security that an at-will employee lacks: the covenant exists to protect the parties' right to receive the benefits of the agreement actually made, and it cannot impose substantive duties or limits beyond the specific terms of that agreement. Because the section 2922 presumption allows an employer to terminate at will, the mere existence of an employment relationship affords no legally protectible expectation that employment will continue or will end only on certain conditions unless the parties have actually adopted such terms; an at-will employer therefore does not frustrate the employee's contractual rights merely by terminating. The court disapproved earlier Court of Appeal decisions to the extent they suggested the covenant could limit termination rights beyond those expressed or implied in fact in the contract. Guz also confirmed the remedial rule from Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988): where personnel policies have become implied-in-fact contract terms, failing to follow them when terminating an employee is a breach of the contract itself, but a claim that merely realleges that breach as a violation of the covenant is superfluous, the remedy for breach of an employment agreement (including its implied covenant) is solely contractual, and allegations that the breach was wrongful, in bad faith, arbitrary, and unfair are unavailing because "there is no tort of 'bad faith breach' of an employment contract." Foley itself had held that tort remedies are not available to employees who allege discharge in violation of the implied covenant. For Jordan Lee's separation from Acme, Inc., this means that any claim based on the covenant would rise or fall with the existence and terms of an actual contract, express or implied in fact.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The mere existence of an employment relationship affords no expectation, protectible by law, that employment will continue, or will end only on certain conditions, unless the parties have actually adopted such terms. Thus if the employer’s termination decisions, however arbitrary, do not breach such a substantive contract provision, they are not precluded by the covenant."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 350 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Of course, as we have indicated above, the employer’s personnel policies and practices may become implied-in-fact terms of the contract between employer and employee. If that has occurred, the employer’s failure to follow such policies when terminating an employee is a breach of the contract itself."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 352 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "Allegations that the breach was wrongful, in bad faith, arbitrary, and unfair are unavailing; there is no tort of “bad faith breach” of an employment contract."
  — Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317, 24 Cal.4th 317, 352 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2569285/guz-v-bechtel-national-inc/)
  "we hold that tort remedies are not available for breach of the implied covenant in an employment contract to employees who allege they have been discharged in violation of the covenant."
  — Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654, 47 Cal.3d 654, 700 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1170824/foley-v-interactive-data-corp/)
  Known gap: This clause combines Guz's holding on the scope of the implied covenant in employment (Part III.C of the opinion) with Foley's holding on remedies, used as real evidence of both rules — not a claim about whether any particular employer breached a contract or acted in bad faith. Guz notes an exception it did not decide (its footnote 18, referenced in the text as "But see fn. 18, post") concerning whether the covenant might be implicated where an employer terminates an at-will employee to cheat the employee of compensation already earned; that footnote was not retrieved for this document and its content is not described here. The disapproved Court of Appeal decisions (Rulon-Miller, Gray, Khanna, Pugh in part, Cleary, and the Ninth Circuit's Kern decision) are identified only as Guz identified them. The Foley quotation is the court's statement of its holding in the opinion's concluding section; Foley's separate holdings on the plaintiff's public-policy and implied-contract claims are outside this clause. Quote-verification note: the Guz text uses typographic quotation marks around "bad faith breach"; those are reproduced in the quote below.

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., recorded here as beginning on March 3, 2014 and ending on August 28, 2026. It describes what California's Labor Code and the California Supreme Court have said about the default rule that employment with no specified term may be ended at the will of either party (Labor Code section 2922), about how the parties to an employment relationship can depart from that default by an express or implied-in-fact agreement limiting the employer's right to terminate, about the kinds of evidence courts consider when deciding whether such an implied agreement exists, and about the limits of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing as a separate source of protection. Whether Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. actually reached any understanding that departed from at-will employment, what Acme, Inc.'s personnel documents said, and why the employment ended on August 28, 2026 are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and dates here does not itself establish that any of the rules described below applies to their relationship, and this sheet states what the statute and the courts have said rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular separation.

Labor Code section 2922 states the default rule for California employment relationships: an employment that has no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other, and "employment for a specified term" means employment for a period greater than one month. In Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000), the California Supreme Court described what that default means in practice — an at-will employment may be ended by either party "at any time without cause," for any or no reason, subject to no procedure except the statutory requirement of notice — and, in the part of the opinion addressing the implied covenant of good faith, stated the consequence bluntly: where the presumption applies, the employer may act peremptorily, arbitrarily, or inconsistently, without providing protections such as prior warning, fair procedures, objective evaluation, or preferential reassignment. The court characterized this statutory presumption as "strong." As applied to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., this clause states the default from which the analysis in the following clauses begins; whether that default was displaced by an express or implied agreement is a separate question those clauses address.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause combines the statutory text of Labor Code section 2922 with the California Supreme Court's description of the at-will default in Guz. It is real evidence of what the default rule is, not a claim that any particular employee is or was at-will, and not a claim that the default is unlimited: Guz itself immediately notes that the presumption "is subject to several limitations," and California has separate statutory and common-law rules (for example, anti-discrimination and anti-retaliation statutes, and the tort of wrongful termination in violation of public policy) that restrict the reasons for which even an at-will employee may be discharged; those are addressed in other documents in this corpus, not here. The Guz quotations come from the opinion's discussion of Labor Code section 2922 in Part III.A and from its discussion of the implied covenant in Part III.C; the second quotation describes the employer's latitude under the presumption "a fortiori" as a step in the court's reasoning about the covenant, and is reproduced here for what it says about the presumption. expectedJSON.body: Guz explains that the section 2922 presumption governs only where the employer and employee "have reached no other understanding." Because the employment relationship is fundamentally contractual, the statute does not overcome the parties' freedom of contract to depart from at-will employment, and it does not prevent them from agreeing to any limitation, otherwise lawful, on the employer's termination rights. The court described the range of what can be agreed: the parties may define for themselves what cause or causes will permit termination, may specify the procedures under which termination shall occur, and may restrict the employer's termination rights more in some situations while leaving the employer freer in others. One familiar example is an agreement that the employee will be discharged only for "good cause," which the court, quoting its earlier decision in Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co., described as "a fair and honest cause or reason, regulated by good faith," as opposed to one that is "trivial, capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual." Whether Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee reached any such understanding — express or implied — is a question of fact this clause does not resolve.

The court's phrasing ("otherwise lawful") signals that some agreed limits could themselves be unlawful; this clause does not catalogue which. The "good cause" definition is quoted as Guz itself quoted it from Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. expectedJSON.body: The agreement that displaces at-will status does not have to be written or even spoken. Guz confirms that the contractual understanding "may be implied in fact, arising from the parties' conduct evidencing their actual mutual intent to create such enforceable limitations." The kinds of evidence that bear on whether such an implied agreement exists, and what its content is, were identified by the California Supreme Court in Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988), which drew them from the Court of Appeal's earlier decision in Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc. (1981): the personnel policies or practices of the employer, the employee's longevity of service, actions or communications by the employer reflecting assurances of continued employment, and the practices of the industry in which the employee is engaged. Foley added that, under Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary the relationship is terminable at any time without cause — but that when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, section 2922 does not diminish the force of those obligations. As applied here, these are the categories of evidence a court would look to in deciding whether Acme, Inc.'s conduct toward Jordan Lee between March 3, 2014 and August 28, 2026 evidenced an actual mutual understanding limiting termination; the clauses that follow describe how Guz said that evidence is weighed.

But when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, Labor Code section 2922 does not diminish the force of such contractual or legal obligations.

expectedJSON.body: Guz clarified how the Foley factors operate. Foley had said the "totality of the circumstances" must be examined; Guz explained that this does not mean that any vague combination of factors, "shaken together in a bag," necessarily allows a finding that the employee could be discharged only for good cause. Instead, courts "seek to enforce the actual understanding" of the parties, and the exact terms to which they assented — whether by express words or by conduct evidencing a similar meeting of minds — receive equally precise scrutiny. The court then stated the operative test for cases with no express agreement: every case turns on its own facts; the issue is whether the other evidence of the parties' conduct has a "tendency in reason" to demonstrate the existence of an actual mutual understanding on particular terms and conditions of employment; if that evidence logically permits conflicting inferences, a question of fact is presented; but where the undisputed facts negate the existence or breach of the claimed contract, summary judgment is proper. Whether the evidence concerning Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. would permit conflicting inferences is a question this clause describes but does not answer.

If such evidence logically permits conflicting inferences, a question of fact is presented.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the California Supreme Court's own explanation of how the implied-contract inquiry is conducted, used as real evidence of the standard — not a prediction of how any particular set of facts would come out. The court's reference to Evidence Code section 210 (which defines relevant evidence in terms of a "tendency in reason") is reproduced from the opinion; section 210 was not independently fetched for this document. The summary-judgment sentence reflects the procedural posture of Guz (review of a summary judgment) and states when that procedure is proper, not what a jury would find at trial.

expectedJSON.body: One of Guz's most-cited holdings concerns the "longevity of service" factor. John Guz had worked for Bechtel for over twenty years with steady raises, promotions, commendations, and good performance reviews, and argued that this record was strong evidence of an implied contract for permanent employment except upon good cause. The California Supreme Court agreed with a line of post-Foley Court of Appeal decisions that such events are "but natural consequences of a well-functioning employment relationship" and held that an employee's mere passage of time in the employer's service — even where marked with tangible indicia that the employer approves the employee's work — cannot alone form an implied-in-fact contract that the employee is no longer at will. Absent other evidence of the employer's intent, the court said, longevity, raises and promotions "are their own rewards" and do not, in and of themselves, constitute a contractual guarantee of future employment security; a contrary rule "would discourage the retention and promotion of employees." The court was equally clear that long service is not irrelevant: over an employee's tenure the employer can communicate, by its written and unwritten policies and practices or by informal assurances, that seniority and longevity do create rights against termination at will, and the issue is whether the employer's words or conduct, on which the employee reasonably relied, gave rise to that specific understanding. The length of Jordan Lee's service with Acme, Inc. from March 3, 2014 to August 28, 2026 is therefore a fact this doctrine treats as relevant only in combination with such words or conduct.

citations.case: Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317
citations.quote: We agree that an employee’s mere passage of time in the employer’s service, even where marked with tangible indicia that the employer approves the employee’s work, cannot alone form an implied-in-fact contract that the employee is no longer at will. Absent other evidence of the employer’s intent, longevity, raises and promotions are their own rewards for the employee’s continuing valued service; they do not, in and of themselves, additionally constitute a contractual guarantee of future employment security. A rule granting such contract rights on the basis of successful longevity alone would discourage the retention and promotion of employees.

The issue is whether the employer’s words or conduct, on which an employee reasonably relied, gave rise to that specific understanding.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the California Supreme Court's holding on the weight of longevity, raises, promotions, and favorable reviews, used as real evidence of that rule — not a determination that any particular employee's service record does or does not support an implied contract. The court's characterization of the post-Foley Court of Appeal decisions (Horn, Kovatch, Davis, Tollefson, Miller) is reproduced as Guz summarized them; those decisions were not independently fetched. Guz also expressly declined to read Foley as holding that long service alone suffices, explaining that Foley's own plaintiff had alleged "repeated oral assurances of job security" in addition to six years and nine months of service; Foley's own sentence on length of service is quoted below from the Foley text, and Guz's discussion of it is summarized in the body. expectedJSON.body: Guz addressed two kinds of employer documents that often point in opposite directions. Bechtel's written policy stated that its employees had no agreements guaranteeing continuous service and could be terminated at the company's option, and Bechtel argued this disclaimer conclusively reinforced the statutory presumption. The court held that an express disclaimer, reinforced by the presumption, satisfied the employer's initial burden on summary judgment, but did not necessarily foreclose the employee from proving an implied agreement: disclaimer language in a handbook or policy manual "does not necessarily mean an employee is employed at will." At the same time, such a disclaimer cannot be ignored — like any direct expression of employer intent communicated to employees and intended to apply to them, it must be taken into account along with all other pertinent evidence in ascertaining the terms of employment. Conversely, the court recognized that an employer's written personnel policies "may be an important source of implied-contract evidence," adding that when an employer promulgates formal personnel policies in handbooks, manuals, and memoranda disseminated to employees, "a strong inference may arise" that the employer intended workers to rely on them as terms and conditions of employment and that employees reasonably did so, and reiterating Foley's statement that a trier of fact can infer an agreement to limit the grounds for termination based on the employee's reasonable reliance on the company's personnel manual or policies. On the facts before it, the court found triable evidence that Bechtel's written personnel documents set forth implied contractual limits on the circumstances of termination, while also holding that those documents did not restrict Bechtel's freedom to reorganize and reduce its work force: Bechtel had "the absolute right" to eliminate Guz's work unit even if the decision was influenced by dissatisfaction with the unit's performance and even if the documents entitled an individual employee to progressive discipline before being fired for poor performance. What Acme, Inc.'s handbook, policies, and disclaimers (if any) said, and whether Jordan Lee reasonably relied on them, are facts this clause does not establish.

But neither the disclaimer nor the statutory presumption necessarily foreclosed Guz from proving the existence and breach of such an agreement.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause reports the California Supreme Court's treatment of handbook disclaimers and written personnel policies as real evidence of how such documents are weighed — not a claim about what any particular employer's documents provide or whether an employee relied on them. The court's discussion of out-of-state and lower-court authority on handbook disclaimers (Thomka, Walker, Wilkerson, Wood, and others) is reflected only through the court's own summary and was not independently fetched. The sentence about reasonable reliance on a personnel manual is Guz quoting Foley (47 Cal.3d at pp. 681-682); it is quoted here as it appears in the Guz text. The quoted "absolute right" sentence reflects the court's reading of Bechtel's specific personnel documents, which did not address reorganizations; it is not a general rule that written policies can never limit an employer's reorganization decisions. Guz left for the Court of Appeal on remand whether Bechtel breached the fair-layoff provisions (objective ranking, placement assistance) in its written policies; that question was not decided in the opinion quoted here.

expectedJSON.body: Every California contract, including an employment contract, carries an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Guz explained why that covenant cannot itself supply the job security that an at-will employee lacks: the covenant exists to protect the parties' right to receive the benefits of the agreement actually made, and it cannot impose substantive duties or limits beyond the specific terms of that agreement. Because the section 2922 presumption allows an employer to terminate at will, the mere existence of an employment relationship affords no legally protectible expectation that employment will continue or will end only on certain conditions unless the parties have actually adopted such terms; an at-will employer therefore does not frustrate the employee's contractual rights merely by terminating. The court disapproved earlier Court of Appeal decisions to the extent they suggested the covenant could limit termination rights beyond those expressed or implied in fact in the contract. Guz also confirmed the remedial rule from Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988): where personnel policies have become implied-in-fact contract terms, failing to follow them when terminating an employee is a breach of the contract itself, but a claim that merely realleges that breach as a violation of the covenant is superfluous, the remedy for breach of an employment agreement (including its implied covenant) is solely contractual, and allegations that the breach was wrongful, in bad faith, arbitrary, and unfair are unavailing because "there is no tort of 'bad faith breach' of an employment contract." Foley itself had held that tort remedies are not available to employees who allege discharge in violation of the implied covenant. For Jordan Lee's separation from Acme, Inc., this means that any claim based on the covenant would rise or fall with the existence and terms of an actual contract, express or implied in fact.

citations.quote: The mere existence of an employment relationship affords no expectation, protectible by law, that employment will continue, or will end only on certain conditions, unless the parties have actually adopted such terms. Thus if the employer’s termination decisions, however arbitrary, do not breach such a substantive contract provision, they are not precluded by the covenant.

citations.case: Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317
citations.quote: Of course, as we have indicated above, the employer’s personnel policies and practices may become implied-in-fact terms of the contract between employer and employee. If that has occurred, the employer’s failure to follow such policies when terminating an employee is a breach of the contract itself.

citations.case: Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317
citations.quote: Allegations that the breach was wrongful, in bad faith, arbitrary, and unfair are unavailing; there is no tort of “bad faith breach” of an employment contract.

citations.case: Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654
citations.quote: we hold that tort remedies are not available for breach of the implied covenant in an employment contract to employees who allege they have been discharged in violation of the covenant.

The Foley quotation is the court's statement of its holding in the opinion's concluding section; Foley's separate holdings on the plaintiff's public-policy and implied-contract claims are outside this clause.
